articles.description: The information technology industry is driving massive growth in global electricity demand, which is set to rise by more than 10,000 TWh over the next ten years. In its World Energy Outlook released this week, the International Energy Agency once again joined the growing chorus of forecasters warning that data centers are becoming a major drain on electricity supply. articles.title: Wind Could Cut the Cost of Round-the-Clock Solar Power by 18%, Ember Says
articles.description: A new report from Ember Energy shows the enormous cost-saving potential of wind energy. While solar power and battery storage have taken off on a global level, wind power has been slower to expand. articles.title: Trump’s Coal Revival Is Costing Americans More Than Expected
articles.description: United States President Trump has doubled down on his support for fossil fuels since coming into office almost two years ago, including the most polluting of them all – coal. Just as many coal plants were on their way to retirement, Trump stepped in and stopped them from closing, backing his decision with federal funds. Recent assessments suggest that the move has cost U.S. taxpayers billions of dollars with little to show for it. articles.title: Thanksgiving Gas Prices Could Break a Record Despite Recent Plunge
articles.description: Gasoline prices have fallen nearly 60 cents in a month, but Americans heading out for Thanksgiving could still pay more at the pump than during any previous Thanksgiving. The national average fell to $3.69 per gallon on Friday, according to AAA, down from approximately $4.30 a month ago. GasBuddy expects prices to average $3.62 on Thanksgiving Day, which would surpass the previous holiday record of $3.56 set in 2022. The declines are substantial. articles.title: US Data Center Boom Faces a New Political Reality
articles.description: Starting in January, Democratic governors will lead US states that together hold 77% of the 300 gigawatts (GW) of data center capacity announced for 2027-2030, including the five largest markets: Texas, Virginia, Pennsylvania, Ohio and Georgia. Most of the winning candidates campaigned on making data centers pay their grid costs, rather than on stopping them, so the midterms are likely to change the terms of growth more than its pace.
